items.title: The annihilator of a module over an enveloping algebra
items.statement: Let $\mathfrak g$ be a complex Lie algebra and let $M$ be a nonzero left $U(\mathfrak g)$-module with action $\rho_M\colon U(\mathfrak g)\to\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(M)$. The annihilator of $M$ is $$\operatorname{Ann}_{U(\mathfrak g)}(M)=\{u\in U(\mathfrak g): um=0\text{ for every }m\in M\}=\ker\rho_M,$$ and for $m\in M$ one writes $\operatorname{Ann}(m)=\{u:um=0\}$. Then $\operatorname{Ann}_{U(\mathfrak g)}(M)$ is a two-sided ideal of $U(\mathfrak g)$, equal to the intersection of the left ideals $\operatorname{Ann}(m)$, $m\in M$; the action descends to a faithful action of the quotient algebra $U(\mathfrak g)/\operatorname{Ann}_{U(\mathfrak g)}(M)$ on $M$.
items.strategy: Unwind the definitions. The annihilator of the whole module is exactly the kernel of the algebra homomorphism $\rho_M$, hence a two-sided ideal by the kernel theorem for ring homomorphisms; the pointwise description follows by intersecting the pointwise kernels. The induced action of the quotient is faithful by construction, and the quotient acts by the same formula.

references.title: P. Etingof, Representations of Lie Groups (18.757, MIT OCW 2023 full notes)
D. Barbasch, Cells in Weyl groups and primitive ideals (AIM workshop notes, 2006)

items.title: Primitive ideals of an enveloping algebra
items.statement:
Let $\mathfrak g$ be a complex Lie algebra. A two-sided ideal
$I\mathrel{\trianglelefteq}U(\mathfrak g)$ ([[def-left-right-and-two-sided-ideal]])
is **primitive** if there exists a simple left $U(\mathfrak g)$-module $M$
([[def-simple-module]]) with

$$I=\operatorname{Ann}_{U(\mathfrak g)}(M)=\{u\in U(\mathfrak g):um=0\text{ for every }m\in M\}$$

([[def-annihilator-ideal-of-a-lie-algebra-module]]). Equivalently: a two-sided
ideal is primitive if it is the kernel of the action of $U(\mathfrak g)$ on some
simple module. Every primitive ideal is proper, and $U(\mathfrak g)/I$ admits the faithful
simple module $M$; no highest-weight hypothesis is imposed on $M$.
items.strategy: Definition: combine the annihilator definition with simplicity of the module. Properness follows because $1$ acts as the identity on a nonzero module, so $1\notin I$. Faithfulness of the quotient action on $M$ is the last part of the annihilator definition. The equivalent kernel formulation is the same statement.

references.title: P. Etingof, Representations of Lie Groups (18.757, MIT OCW 2023 full notes)
D. Barbasch, Cells in Weyl groups and primitive ideals (AIM workshop notes, 2006)

items.title: Annihilators of simple highest-weight modules are primitive
items.statement: Let $\mathfrak g$ be a finite-dimensional complex semisimple Lie algebra, let $\lambda\in\mathfrak h^*$, let $M(\lambda)$ be the Verma module of highest weight $\lambda$, and let $L(\lambda)$ be its unique simple quotient. Then $I(\lambda):=\operatorname{Ann}_{U(\mathfrak g)}(L(\lambda))$ is a primitive ideal of $U(\mathfrak g)$; moreover $\operatorname{Ann}_{U(\mathfrak g)}M(\lambda)\subseteq I(\lambda)$, with equality whenever $M(\lambda)$ is simple (in which case $L(\lambda)\cong M(\lambda)$).
items.strategy: The unique-simple-quotient theorem supplies a nonzero simple module $L(\lambda)$, so its annihilator is primitive by definition. Since $L(\lambda)$ is a quotient of $M(\lambda)$, every operator annihilating $M(\lambda)$ annihilates the quotient, which gives the inclusion. If $M(\lambda)$ is itself simple, then $L(\lambda)\cong M(\lambda)$ and the annihilators coincide.

references.title: P. Etingof, Representations of Lie Groups (18.757, MIT OCW 2023 full notes)
D. Barbasch, Cells in Weyl groups and primitive ideals (AIM workshop notes, 2006)

items.title: Primitive ideals are prime in the noncommutative sense
items.statement: Let $I$ be a primitive ideal of $U(\mathfrak g)$ and let $A,B$ be two-sided ideals of $U(\mathfrak g)$ with $AB\subseteq I$. Then $A\subseteq I$ or $B\subseteq I$. The claim holds for every complex Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$, and equivalently the quotient ring $U(\mathfrak g)/I$ is prime.
items.strategy: Choose a simple left module $M$ with $I=\operatorname{Ann}M$. If $B\not\subseteq I$, then $BM\neq0$, and $BM$ is a submodule of the simple module $M$, so $BM=M$. Then $AM=A(BM)=(AB)M\subseteq IM=0$, hence $A\subseteq\operatorname{Ann}M=I$. Thus failure of $B\subseteq I$ forces $A\subseteq I$. Use the product of ideals and its closure under the usual operations.

references.title: P. Etingof, Representations of Lie Groups (18.757, MIT OCW 2023 full notes)
D. Barbasch, Cells in Weyl groups and primitive ideals (AIM workshop notes, 2006)

items.title: Dixmier's lemma: endomorphisms of a simple module over a countable-dimensional algebra
items.statement: Let $A$ be a unital $\mathbb C$-algebra which admits a countable $\mathbb C$-basis, and let $M$ be a simple left $A$-module. Then every $A$-endomorphism of $M$ is multiplication by a scalar: $\operatorname{End}_A(M)=\mathbb C\cdot\operatorname{id}_M$. Consequently the center $Z(A)$ acts on $M$ by scalars and there is a unital $\mathbb C$-algebra homomorphism $\chi\colon Z(A)\to\mathbb C$ with $zm=\chi(z)m$ for all $z\in Z(A)$, $m\in M$. In particular this applies to $A=U(\mathfrak g)$ for a finite-dimensional complex Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$.
items.strategy: Schur's lemma makes $D=\operatorname{End}_A(M)$ a division ring containing $\mathbb C$. An element $x\in D\setminus\mathbb C$ is transcendental over the algebraically closed field $\mathbb C$: an algebraic element satisfies a split polynomial over $\mathbb C$, and a product of nonzero factors in a division ring is nonzero. Hence $D$ contains the rational function field $\mathbb C(x)$, in which the elements $1/(x-a)$, $a\in\mathbb C$, are $\mathbb C$-linearly independent: a finite relation multiplied by $\prod_i(x-a_i)$ and evaluated at $a_j$ isolates $c_j\prod_{i\neq j}(a_j-a_i)=0$. On the other hand, for $0\neq v\in M$ the evaluation map $D\to M$, $T\mapsto Tv$, is injective because $M=Av$ and $T=0$ on $v$ forces $T=0$; and $M$, as a quotient of the countable-dimensional space $A$, is a countable union of finite-dimensional subspaces, which cannot contain an uncountable linearly independent set. Therefore $D=\mathbb C$. For $z\in Z(A)$ the map $m\mapsto zm$ is an $A$-endomorphism, hence a scalar $\chi(z)$, and $\chi$ is a unital algebra homomorphism because the module is nonzero. Use PBW to see that $U(\mathfrak g)$ is countable-dimensional for finite-dimensional $\mathfrak g$.

references.title: P. Etingof, Representations of Lie Groups (18.757, MIT OCW 2023 full notes)

items.title: A primitive ideal determines a central character
items.statement: Let $\mathfrak g$ be a finite-dimensional complex Lie algebra and let $I$ be a primitive ideal of $U(\mathfrak g)$, say $I=\operatorname{Ann}_{U(\mathfrak g)}(M)$ with $M$ simple. Then $Z(U(\mathfrak g))$ acts on $M$ by a central character $\chi_I\colon Z(U(\mathfrak g))\to\mathbb C$, and $$I\cap Z(U(\mathfrak g))=\ker\chi_I.$$ In particular $I\cap Z(U(\mathfrak g))$ is a maximal ideal of the commutative algebra $Z(U(\mathfrak g))$, and $U(\mathfrak g)\ker\chi_I\subseteq I$.
items.strategy: Dixmier's lemma gives the central character: every central element acts on the simple module $M$ by a scalar, and the scalars assemble into a unital algebra homomorphism $\chi_I$. If $z\in I\cap Z$, then $z$ acts as $0$ and as $\chi_I(z)$, so $\chi_I(z)=0$ because $M\neq0$. Conversely, if $z\in\ker\chi_I$, then $z$ acts as $0$ on $M$, so $z\in I$. Hence $I\cap Z=\ker\chi_I$. This ideal is maximal because $\chi_I$ is a unital homomorphism onto the field $\mathbb C$, so $Z/\ker\chi_I\cong\mathbb C$ is a field. Finally $z\in\ker\chi_I$ lies in the two-sided ideal $I$, so the two-sided ideal $U(\mathfrak g)\ker\chi_I$ is contained in $I$.

references.title: P. Etingof, Representations of Lie Groups (18.757, MIT OCW 2023 full notes)
D. Barbasch, Cells in Weyl groups and primitive ideals (AIM workshop notes, 2006)

items.title: The central reduction of the enveloping algebra at a central character
items.statement: Let $\chi\colon Z(U(\mathfrak g))\to\mathbb C$ be a central character of $U(\mathfrak g)$ and let $U(\mathfrak g)\ker\chi$ be the two-sided ideal generated by the kernel of $\chi$. The central reduction of $U(\mathfrak g)$ at $\chi$ is the quotient algebra $$U_\chi:=U(\mathfrak g)\,/\,U(\mathfrak g)\ker\chi.$$ It is a unital associative $\mathbb C$-algebra, the natural map $U(\mathfrak g)\to U_\chi$ is a surjective algebra homomorphism with kernel $U(\mathfrak g)\ker\chi$, the image of $Z(U(\mathfrak g))$ in $U_\chi$ is $\mathbb C\cdot1$, and for a $U(\mathfrak g)$-module $M$ the following are equivalent: (i) $M$ has central character $\chi$; (ii) $\ker\chi$ annihilates $M$; (iii) the action of $U(\mathfrak g)$ on $M$ factors uniquely through $U_\chi$. Thus the $U(\mathfrak g)$-modules with central character $\chi$ are exactly the $U_\chi$-modules.
items.strategy: Definitions plus the universal property of quotients. The ideal $U(\mathfrak g)\ker\chi$ is two-sided because it is generated by a set of central elements. A module on which every $z-\chi(z)$ acts by zero is the same as a module killed by $\ker\chi$, equivalently a module for the quotient; the factorization is unique because the quotient map is surjective. On the quotient, every central element acts by its scalar, so the image of the center is the scalars.

references.title: P. Etingof, Representations of Lie Groups (18.757, MIT OCW 2023 full notes)
D. Barbasch, Cells in Weyl groups and primitive ideals (AIM workshop notes, 2006)

items.title: The Verma annihilator contains the central-character ideal
items.statement: Let $\lambda\in\mathfrak h^*$, let $\chi_\lambda\colon Z(U(\mathfrak g))\to\mathbb C$ be the central character determined by $\lambda$ through the Harish-Chandra projection, so that every $z\in Z(U(\mathfrak g))$ acts on the Verma module $M(\lambda)$ by the scalar $\chi_\lambda(z)=\operatorname{pr}(z)(\lambda)$. Then $$U(\mathfrak g)\ker\chi_\lambda\subseteq\operatorname{Ann}_{U(\mathfrak g)}M(\lambda)\subseteq\operatorname{Ann}_{U(\mathfrak g)}L(\lambda)=I(\lambda),$$ and every element of the two-sided ideal generated by $\ker\chi_\lambda$ annihilates every cyclic highest-weight module of highest weight $\lambda$.
items.strategy: The central elements act on the cyclic highest-weight module $M(\lambda)$ by scalars, and the Harish-Chandra projection computes the scalar as $\operatorname{pr}(z)(\lambda)=\chi_\lambda(z)$; hence $\ker\chi_\lambda$ annihilates $M(\lambda)$. Since an annihilator is a two-sided ideal, this gives $U(\mathfrak g)\ker\chi_\lambda\subseteq\operatorname{Ann}M(\lambda)$. The second inclusion holds because $L(\lambda)$ is a quotient of $M(\lambda)$: an operator annihilating $M(\lambda)$ annihilates every quotient.

references.title: P. Etingof, Representations of Lie Groups (18.757, MIT OCW 2023 full notes)
D. Barbasch, Cells in Weyl groups and primitive ideals (AIM workshop notes, 2006)

items.title: The adjoint action preserves the associated graded of a two-sided ideal
items.statement:
Let $\mathfrak g$ be a finite-dimensional complex Lie algebra with the PBW
filtration $F^nU(\mathfrak g)$, $n\ge0$, and the identification
$\operatorname{gr}U(\mathfrak g)=S(\mathfrak g)$. For every two-sided ideal
$I\subseteq U(\mathfrak g)$ the associated graded subspace

$$\operatorname{gr}I=\bigoplus_{n\ge0}\bigl(I\cap F^nU(\mathfrak g)\bigr)\big/\bigl(I\cap F^{n-1}U(\mathfrak g)\bigr)\subseteq S(\mathfrak g)$$

is a graded ideal of $S(\mathfrak g)$. Moreover, writing $D_x$ for the
derivation of $S(\mathfrak g)$ that extends the linear map
$\operatorname{ad}_x\colon\mathfrak g\to\mathfrak g$, $y\mapsto[x,y]$
([[def-derivation-of-a-lie-algebra]]), one has
$D_x(\operatorname{gr}I)\subseteq\operatorname{gr}I$ for every $x\in\mathfrak g$,
and, with $\sigma_n\colon F^nU(\mathfrak g)\to F^nU(\mathfrak g)/F^{n-1}U(\mathfrak g)$ the degree-$n$ quotient map, the induced derivation satisfies:

$$\sigma_n(\operatorname{ad}_xu)=D_x(\sigma_n(u)),\qquad \operatorname{ad}_xu=xu-ux,$$

for every $n\ge0$ and $u\in F^nU(\mathfrak g)$. If the commutator has degree less than $n$, its degree-$n$ symbol is zero.
items.strategy: Use the degree-n quotient map sigma_n. The commutator preserves each PBW filtration level and the two-sided ideal; the induced graded derivation agrees on generators with D_x and hence agrees everywhere. Its invariance preserves gr I even when the commutator drops degree.

references.title: D. Barbasch, Cells in Weyl groups and primitive ideals (AIM workshop notes, 2006)
D. A. Vogan, The orbit method and primitive ideals for semisimple Lie algebras (CMS Conf. Proc. 1986)

items.title: The associated graded variety of a two-sided ideal
items.statement: Let $\mathfrak g$ be a finite-dimensional complex Lie algebra and let $I\subseteq U(\mathfrak g)$ be a two-sided ideal. Its associated graded ideal is $\operatorname{gr}I\subseteq\operatorname{gr}U(\mathfrak g)=S(\mathfrak g)$, and $S(\mathfrak g)$ is identified with the polynomial functions on $\mathfrak g^*$ via a chosen basis, so the associated variety of $I$ is the classical affine algebraic set $$\mathcal V(I):=V(\operatorname{gr}I)=\{\xi\in\mathfrak g^*:f(\xi)=0\text{ for every }f\in\operatorname{gr}I\};$$ it is Zariski closed in $\mathfrak g^*$. Since $\operatorname{gr}I$ has no component in degree zero when $I$ is proper, $0\in\mathcal V(I)$; $\mathcal V(I)=\mathfrak g^*$ holds exactly for $I=0$, and $\mathcal V(I)$ is the zero set of the homogeneous generators of $\operatorname{gr}I$.
items.strategy: Define $\operatorname{gr}I$ by the induced filtration $(I\cap F^nU(\mathfrak g))_n$, transport the PBW identification $\operatorname{gr}U(\mathfrak g)=S(\mathfrak g)$ and the polynomial-function model of the coordinate ring of $\mathfrak g^*$, and apply the zero-locus construction for ideals in a polynomial ring. The membership of the origin is the vanishing of all positive-degree polynomials at $0$, and the case of the zero ideal is the definition of the empty set of equations.

references.title: D. Barbasch, Cells in Weyl groups and primitive ideals (AIM workshop notes, 2006)
D. A. Vogan, The orbit method and primitive ideals for semisimple Lie algebras (CMS Conf. Proc. 1986)

items.title: The associated variety is a closed conical coadjoint-invariant cone
items.statement: Let $\mathfrak g$ be a finite-dimensional complex Lie algebra and let $I\subseteq U(\mathfrak g)$ be a two-sided ideal. Then $\mathcal V(I)\subseteq\mathfrak g^*$ is a closed cone: for $\xi\in\mathcal V(I)$ and $t\in\mathbb C$ one has $t\xi\in\mathcal V(I)$. Moreover $\mathcal V(I)$ is invariant under the coadjoint action: for every $x\in\mathfrak g$ and $\xi\in\mathcal V(I)$ the curve $t\mapsto\xi\circ e^{-t\,\operatorname{ad}_x}$ (the exponential of $-t\operatorname{ad}_x$, a one-parameter subgroup of linear automorphisms of $\mathfrak g^*$) stays inside $\mathcal V(I)$. In particular the same conclusions hold for every primitive ideal.
items.strategy: Gradedness of $\operatorname{gr}I$ makes the zero set a cone: a polynomial relation vanishes on $t\xi$ by homogeneity. For coadjoint invariance, let $D_x$ be the derivation of $S(\mathfrak g)=\mathbb C[\mathfrak g^*]$ extending $\operatorname{ad}_x$; it preserves $\operatorname{gr}I$ by the preceding lemma. A finite-dimensional norm majorizes the matrix-exponential series by the scalar exponential series, so $p(t)=f(\xi\circ e^{-t\operatorname{ad}_x})$ is entire; its derivatives at zero are $(-1)^k(D_x^kf)(\xi)$ by termwise differentiation and the chain rule. These vanish because $D_x^kf\in\operatorname{gr}I$ and $\xi\in\mathcal V(I)$, and the global Taylor theorem gives $p\equiv0$.

references.title: D. Barbasch, Cells in Weyl groups and primitive ideals (AIM workshop notes, 2006)
D. A. Vogan, The orbit method and primitive ideals for semisimple Lie algebras (CMS Conf. Proc. 1986)

items.title: Every central character of a semisimple enveloping algebra arises from a weight
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\mathfrak g$ be a finite-dimensional complex
semisimple Lie algebra with Cartan subalgebra $\mathfrak h$ and a fixed positive
system. Then every unital $\mathbb C$-algebra homomorphism
$\chi\colon Z(U(\mathfrak g))\to\mathbb C$ equals $\chi_\lambda$ for some
$\lambda\in\mathfrak h^*$, where $\chi_\lambda(z)=\operatorname{pr}(z)(\lambda)$;
equivalently, the maximal ideals of $Z(U(\mathfrak g))$ are exactly the kernels
$\ker\chi_\lambda$, and $\lambda\mapsto\ker\chi_\lambda$ induces a bijection
$\mathfrak h^*/W\to\operatorname{Max}Z(U(\mathfrak g))$, so that
$\chi_\lambda=\chi_\mu$ if and only if $\mu\in W\cdot\lambda$. Here $w\cdot\lambda=w(\lambda+\rho)-\rho$, and $\mathfrak h^*/W$ denotes the quotient for this dot action.
items.strategy: Compose $\chi$ with the inverse of the Harish-Chandra isomorphism to get a unital homomorphism $\psi\colon S(\mathfrak h)^W\to\mathbb C$; its kernel is maximal. By Chevalley-Shephard-Todd, $S(\mathfrak h)$ is a free, hence finite, module over the polynomial algebra $S(\mathfrak h)^W$. The determinant trick shows that $(\ker\psi)S(\mathfrak h)\neq S(\mathfrak h)$: otherwise $(1-a)S(\mathfrak h)=0$ for some $a\in\ker\psi$, forcing $a=1$. Under Choice a maximal ideal $\mathfrak n$ of $S(\mathfrak h)$ contains $(\ker\psi)S(\mathfrak h)$, and $S(\mathfrak h)/\mathfrak n$ is a finite-dimensional field extension of $S(\mathfrak h)^W/\ker\psi\cong\mathbb C$, hence equals $\mathbb C$; the composite $S(\mathfrak h)\to\mathbb C$ extends $\psi$ and is evaluation at some $\lambda\in\mathfrak h^*$. Then $\chi(z)=\psi(HC_\rho(z))=HC_\rho(z)(\lambda)=\operatorname{pr}(z)(\lambda-\rho)$ in the shifted convention, which is $\chi_{\lambda-\rho}(z)$; for the bijection statement, every maximal ideal of $Z(U(\mathfrak g))$ is the kernel of a unital homomorphism to $\mathbb C$ because $Z(U(\mathfrak g))$ is an affine $\mathbb C$-algebra and $\mathbb C$ is algebraically closed, and the preceding paragraph identifies these kernels with the $\chi_\lambda$; injectivity on $W$-orbits is the published orbit theorem.

references.title: P. Etingof, Representations of Lie Groups (18.757, MIT OCW 2023 full notes)
D. Barbasch, Cells in Weyl groups and primitive ideals (AIM workshop notes, 2006)

items.title: Primitive ideals are partitioned by dot-orbit central characters
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\mathfrak g$ be a finite-dimensional complex semisimple Lie algebra with Cartan subalgebra $\mathfrak h$ and a fixed positive system. If $I$ is a primitive ideal of $U(\mathfrak g)$, then $I\cap Z(U(\mathfrak g))=\ker\chi_I$ for a unique central character $\chi_I$, and there is a unique dot-Weyl orbit $W\cdot\lambda\subseteq\mathfrak h^*$ with $\chi_I=\chi_\lambda$; this orbit is determined by $I$ alone. Consequently, for primitive ideals $I,J$: $I\cap Z=J\cap Z$ if and only if $\chi_I=\chi_J$, if and only if $W\cdot\lambda=W\cdot\mu$ for any $\lambda,\mu$ with $\chi_\lambda=\chi_I$ and $\chi_\mu=\chi_J$. Thus the primitive ideals are partitioned by their central characters, and the central character of a primitive ideal is exactly a dot-Weyl orbit under the Harish-Chandra isomorphism.
items.strategy: Apply the primitive-central-character proposition to write $I\cap Z=\ker\chi_I$; a central character is determined by its kernel, so $\chi_I$ is unique. The parametrization lemma produces $\lambda$ with $\chi_I=\chi_\lambda$, and the published orbit theorem gives $\chi_\lambda=\chi_\mu$ exactly on the dot orbit $W\cdot\lambda$, which therefore is independent of the choice of $\lambda$ and depends only on $I$. The stated equivalences follow.

references.title: P. Etingof, Representations of Lie Groups (18.757, MIT OCW 2023 full notes)
D. Barbasch, Cells in Weyl groups and primitive ideals (AIM workshop notes, 2006)

items.title: The central reduction of U(sl2) is simple away from the finite-dimensional central characters
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\mathfrak g=\mathfrak{sl}_2(\mathbb C)$ with standard basis $e,f,h$, Casimir element $\Omega$, and center $Z(U(\mathfrak g))=\mathbb C[\Omega]$. Let $\chi$ be a central character, determined by the scalar $\chi(\Omega)$. Then the central reduction $U_\chi$ is a simple ring if and only if $\chi$ is not the central character of any nonzero finite-dimensional $U(\mathfrak g)$-module, equivalently if and only if $\chi(\Omega)$ is not the eigenvalue of $\Omega$ on any finite-dimensional simple module $L(n)$, $n\ge0$ (these eigenvalues are pairwise distinct). When $U_\chi$ is simple, every nonzero $U(\mathfrak g)$-module with central character $\chi$ is faithful over $U_\chi$, every Verma module $M(\lambda)$ with $\chi_\lambda=\chi$ is simple, and $\operatorname{Ann}_{U(\mathfrak g)}M(\lambda)=U(\mathfrak g)\ker\chi$.
items.strategy: First normalize the library Casimir by the local Killing-form calculation: Ω=ef+fe+½h²=4C. The line ℂh is Cartan by the bracket relations; its roots are ±α with α(h)=2, so the Weyl reflection acts by sign and S(h)^W=ℂ[h²]. Chevalley restriction and the PBW symbol of C show that σ(C) generates S(g)^g. The graded-adjoint lemma makes σ(z) invariant for every central z; homogeneity makes it a scalar multiple of σ(C)^k, and subtracting the same multiple of C^k lowers PBW degree. Induction proves Z(U(sl2))=ℂ[C]=ℂ[Ω]. In U_χ, write fe=p(h)=-¼(h²+2h-2c) and ef=q(h)=p(h-2). The PBW quotient has Hilbert function 2d+1; degree counting and the generator actions give the normal-form basis {f^i h^a} and {e^j h^a}, so U_χ is infinite-dimensional. Any nonzero two-sided ideal contains a weight vector and hence a nonzero polynomial in h; a least-degree generator P satisfies the two commutator divisibilities. At a root of P, the divisibilities force the last roots of the upward and downward 2-step chains to be roots of p and q. If t^2=1+2c is not an integer square, the terminal-root constraints contradict each other (including t=0), leaving P constant by algebraic closedness of C. If t is a nonzero integer, c=n(n+2)/2 for n=|t|-1 and L(n) gives a nonzero proper kernel in the infinite-dimensional U_χ. Conversely, any nonzero finite-dimensional module with central character χ has a simple submodule, necessarily some L(n), so its central scalar is n(n+2)/2. This proves the simplicity criterion. Simplicity then gives faithfulness of every nonzero U_χ-module; the Verma irreducibility criterion and quotient-kernel description give the final Verma and annihilator claims.

references.title: J. Gaddis, The Weyl algebra and its friends: a survey (arXiv:2305.01609)
R. E. Block, The irreducible representations of the Lie algebra sl(2) and of the Weyl algebra, Adv. Math. 39 (1981) 69-110

items.title: Highest weights can have the same primitive ideal
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) and let $\mathfrak g$ be finite-dimensional complex semisimple. The assignment $\lambda\mapsto I(\lambda)=\operatorname{Ann}_{U(\mathfrak g)}L(\lambda)$
from weights to primitive ideals ([[prop-annihilators-of-simple-highest-weight-modules-are-primitive]],
[[def-primitive-ideal-of-an-enveloping-algebra]],
[[def-annihilator-ideal-of-a-lie-algebra-module]]) is not injective in general,
and a fixed central character can carry more than one primitive ideal;
describing the fibres of this map is the content of Joseph's theory of Goldie
rank polynomials and of Kazhdan-Lusztig cell theory, which is not part of the
algebraic prefix on this page. For noninjectivity, already in $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ the distinct weights $1/2$ and $-5/2$ have normalized Casimir value $5/8$, which is not $n(n+2)/2$ for any integer $n\ge0$: those values are $0$ for $n=0$ and at least $3/2$ for $n\ge1$. By [[lem-the-central-reduction-of-usl2-is-simple-away-from-finite-dimensional-characters]], both Verma modules are simple and have the same annihilator, namely the central ideal. In contrast, the
trivial central character carries the distinct primitive ideals
$\operatorname{Ann}L(0)$ and $\operatorname{Ann}L(-2)$ — the annihilators of
the trivial module and of the simple Verma module $M(-2)=L(-2)$ — so Duflo's
surjectivity is not a bijection between weights and primitive ideals.
items.strategy: Record the boundary: cite the non-uniqueness note that accompanies the classification statement, and the fibre description by character polynomials. No proof is asserted here; the remark prevents overstatement of the surjectivity theorem as a bijection.

references.title: P. Etingof, Representations of Lie Groups (18.757, MIT OCW 2023 full notes)
D. Barbasch, Cells in Weyl groups and primitive ideals (AIM workshop notes, 2006)

title: Primitive Ideals and Duflo Theorem — Examples

items.title: Primitive ideals of U(sl2) at a generic central character
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\mathfrak g=\mathfrak{sl}_2(\mathbb C)$ and let $\chi$ be a central character which is not the central character of any nonzero finite-dimensional $U(\mathfrak g)$-module. Then the central reduction $U_\chi$ is a simple ring, and the unique primitive ideal of $U(\mathfrak g)$ with central character $\chi$ is $U(\mathfrak g)\ker\chi$: for every $\lambda\in\mathfrak h^*$ with $\chi_\lambda=\chi$ the Verma module $M(\lambda)$ is simple and $$\operatorname{Ann}_{U(\mathfrak g)}M(\lambda)=U(\mathfrak g)\ker\chi,$$ so the annihilator is generated by the Casimir relation $\Omega-\chi(\Omega)$ alone. This is the smallest instance of a Duflo annihilator: over a generic central character the primitive ideal is exactly the unavoidable central ideal.
items.strategy: The Axiom of Choice is inherited from [[lem-the-central-reduction-of-usl2-is-simple-away-from-finite-dimensional-characters]]. By the simplicity lemma for the $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ central reduction, $U_\chi$ has no nonzero proper two-sided ideal. For any primitive ideal $I$ with central character $\chi$, the primitive-central-character proposition gives $I\cap Z=\ker\chi$, so $U(\mathfrak g)\ker\chi\subseteq I$; the image of $I$ in the simple ring $U_\chi$ is a two-sided ideal, hence $0$ or $U_\chi$, and it is not $U_\chi$ because $I$ is proper; therefore $I=U(\mathfrak g)\ker\chi$. For $\lambda$ with $\chi_\lambda=\chi$, the Verma module $M(\lambda)$ is simple by the simplicity lemma, so $L(\lambda)=M(\lambda)$, and the annihilator contains $U(\mathfrak g)\ker\chi$; it equals it because $U_\chi$ acts faithfully on the nonzero module $M(\lambda)$.

references.title: P. Etingof, Representations of Lie Groups (18.757, MIT OCW 2023 full notes)
J. Gaddis, The Weyl algebra and its friends: a survey (arXiv:2305.01609)
R. E. Block, The irreducible representations of the Lie algebra sl(2) and of the Weyl algebra, Adv. Math. 39 (1981) 69-110

items.title: The annihilator of the trivial sl(2)-module
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\mathfrak g=\mathfrak{sl}_2(\mathbb C)$ with
standard basis $e,f,h$ and Casimir element $\Omega$, so that
$Z(U(\mathfrak g))=\mathbb C[\Omega]$. The annihilator of the trivial module $\mathbb C$ is
the augmentation ideal
$\operatorname{Ann}_{U(\mathfrak g)}\mathbb C=U(\mathfrak g)\mathfrak g=(e,f,h)$,
the two-sided ideal generated by $\mathfrak g$; it is a primitive ideal whose
central character $\chi_0$ is the one with $\chi_0(\Omega)=0$, and
$\operatorname{Ann}_{U(\mathfrak g)}\mathbb C\cap Z(U(\mathfrak g))=(\Omega)$ is
a maximal ideal of $Z(U(\mathfrak g))$. The central ideal
$U(\mathfrak g)\ker\chi_0=(\Omega)U(\mathfrak g)$ is strictly smaller than the
annihilator: the highest vector of the simple Verma module $M(-2)$ is an
eigenvector of $h$ with eigenvalue $-2$, so $h\in\operatorname{Ann}\mathbb C$
but $h\notin(\Omega)U(\mathfrak g)$. Thus at the trivial central character the
annihilator of the trivial module is not generated by the Casimir relation.
items.strategy: The trivial module acts by the augmentation $\varepsilon\colon U(\mathfrak g)\to\mathbb C$, so its kernel is the augmentation ideal, generated by $\mathfrak g$. The central character sends $\Omega$ to the Casimir eigenvalue of the trivial module, which is $0$, so $\ker\chi_0=(\Omega)$ in $Z(U(\mathfrak g))=\mathbb C[\Omega]$. Since $h$ acts by $0$ on $\mathbb C$ but by $-2$ on the highest vector of the simple Verma module $M(-2)$, the two-sided ideal $(\Omega)U(\mathfrak g)$ does not contain $h$; here $M(-2)$ is a module with central character $\chi_0$, and $(\Omega)U(\mathfrak g)$ annihilates it by the Verma central-character proposition, while $h$ does not.

R. E. Block, The irreducible representations of the Lie algebra sl(2) and of the Weyl algebra, Adv. Math. 39 (1981) 69-110

items.title: The associated variety of a finite-dimensional simple annihilator is the origin
items.statement:
Let $\mathfrak g$ be a finite-dimensional complex semisimple Lie algebra and let
$L(\lambda)$ be a finite-dimensional simple $U(\mathfrak g)$-module, with
$\lambda$ dominant integral. Then
$I(\lambda)=\operatorname{Ann}_{U(\mathfrak g)}L(\lambda)$ has finite codimension
in $U(\mathfrak g)$, and its associated variety is the origin:

$$\mathcal V(I(\lambda))=\{0\}\subseteq\mathfrak g^*.$$ Indeed, with $d=\dim_{\mathbb C}L(\lambda)$, Cayley-Hamilton shows that for every $y\in\mathfrak g$ the power $y^d$ is the symbol of an element of $I(\lambda)$, so $\operatorname{gr}I(\lambda)$ contains the $d$-th powers of all of $\mathfrak g$. Over $\mathbb C$, the polarization identity shows that these pure $d$-th powers span $S^d(\mathfrak g)$: for $y_1,\ldots,y_d\in\mathfrak g$, $$d!\,y_1\cdots y_d=\sum_{J\subseteq\{1,\ldots,d\}}(-1)^{d-|J|} \left(\sum_{j\in J}y_j\right)^d.$$
Since $\operatorname{gr}I(\lambda)$ is an
ideal in $S(\mathfrak g)$, it contains every $S^k(\mathfrak g)$ for $k\ge d$.
Its zero set is therefore $\{0\}$; equivalently, every point $\xi$ in it
satisfies $\xi(y)^d=0$ for all $y\in\mathfrak g$. The finite-dimensionality
of $L(\lambda)$ is essential here. Infinite-dimensional (Verma-type)
annihilators behave differently: their associated varieties need not be
$\{0\}$, and on this page no positive-dimensionality statement about them is
asserted.
items.strategy: The action quotient $U(\mathfrak g)/I(\lambda)$ embeds in the finite-dimensional algebra $\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}L(\lambda)$, so it has finite codimension. Put $d=\dim L(\lambda)$. For each $y\in\mathfrak g$, Cayley--Hamilton for the action of $y$ gives a monic degree-$d$ relation $p_y(y)\in I(\lambda)$ whose leading PBW symbol is $y^d$; hence $y^d\in\operatorname{gr}I(\lambda)$. Polarization over $\mathbb C$ shows that these powers span $S^d(\mathfrak g)$, and the ideal property of $\operatorname{gr}I(\lambda)$ then gives $S^k(\mathfrak g)\subseteq\operatorname{gr}I(\lambda)$ for every $k\ge d$. Thus every point of the associated variety satisfies $\xi(y)^d=0$ for every $y\in\mathfrak g$, so it is the origin; conversely, properness of $I(\lambda)$ puts the origin in the variety. Finite codimension does not imply $F_nU(\mathfrak g)\subseteq I(\lambda)$ for large $n$; the Cayley--Hamilton argument supplies the needed graded statement directly.

references.title: D. Barbasch, Cells in Weyl groups and primitive ideals (AIM workshop notes, 2006)
D. A. Vogan, The orbit method and primitive ideals for semisimple Lie algebras (CMS Conf. Proc. 1986)

items.title: An intersection of two primitive ideals need not be primitive
items.statement: In $U(\mathfrak{sl}_2(\mathbb C))$ the ideals $I_0=\operatorname{Ann}L(0)$ (the trivial module) and $I_1=\operatorname{Ann}L(1)$ (the two-dimensional standard module) are primitive, but their intersection $I_0\cap I_1$ is not primitive. Hence the set of primitive ideals is not closed under finite intersections, and the central-character criterion detects this: $(I_0\cap I_1)\cap Z(U(\mathfrak g))=\ker\chi_0\cap\ker\chi_1$ is not a maximal ideal.
items.strategy: Both annihilators are primitive by the annihilator proposition. Their central intersections are $I_j\cap Z=\ker\chi_j$ by the primitive-central-character proposition, and $\chi_0\neq\chi_1$ because the Casimir eigenvalues of $L(0)$ and $L(1)$ differ. Intersecting the two maximal ideals gives $(I_0\cap I_1)\cap Z=\ker\chi_0\cap\ker\chi_1$, which is strictly contained in the maximal ideal $\ker\chi_0$ and hence is not maximal. By the primitive-central-character proposition a primitive ideal has maximal central intersection, so $I_0\cap I_1$ is not primitive.

items.title: The central character does not determine the primitive ideal
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. In $U(\mathfrak{sl}_2(\mathbb C))$, for every integer $n\ge0$ the primitive ideals $I(n)=\operatorname{Ann}L(n)$ and $J(n)=\operatorname{Ann}M(-n-2)$ are distinct, although $L(n)$ and the simple Verma module $M(-n-2)$ have the same central character $\chi_n=\chi_{-n-2}$. Thus a central character does not determine a unique primitive ideal over it: for $n\ge0$ the fibre of the central-character map on primitive ideals has at least two points, and the assignment $\lambda\mapsto\operatorname{Ann}L(\lambda)$ is not injective. In particular the fibre over the regular integral central character $\chi_0$ already has two points.
items.strategy: Assume equality of the annihilators of L(n) and the simple M(-n-2). The quotient algebra embeds into End_C L(n), so images of its finite basis span the cyclic simple Verma module, contradicting its distinct nonzero weights -n-2-2k. AC is carried from antidominant simplicity and dot-orbit equality. Separately, weights 1/2 and -5/2 have normalized Casimir value 5/8 and identical central-ideal annihilators by the generic simplicity lemma; this proves noninjectivity.
